items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 248: Minutes of directors' meetings
items.quote: The records must be kept for at least ten years from the date of the meeting.
items.why: The binding rule and the source of the figure. Every company must cause minutes of all proceedings at directors' meetings to be recorded and kept for at least ten years; failure is an offence by every officer in default, punishable by a fine. The section does not say what a minute must contain.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 249: Minutes as evidence
items.quote: are evidence (in Scotland, sufficient evidence) of the proceedings at the meeting
items.why: Why the minute book matters in a dispute. Minutes authenticated by the chair of the meeting or of the next meeting are evidence of the proceedings, and until the contrary is proved the meeting is deemed duly held and its proceedings duly to have taken place.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.why: The duty the criterion's top level refers to. A director must act in the way he or she considers, in good faith, most likely to promote the company's success, having regard to long-term consequences, employees, suppliers and customers, the community and environment, and reputation. The section does not mention records or minutes, and no safe harbour appears in it.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CZA: Section 172(1) statement
items.quote: describes how the directors have had regard to the matters set out in section 172(1)(a) to (f)
items.why: The one statutory duty to report on how the section 172 matters were considered. The strategic report must include the statement; it does not apply to a company that qualifies as medium-sized. A board cannot write it honestly without records of what was considered.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 1157: Power of court to grant relief in certain cases
items.quote: he acted honestly and reasonably, and that having regard to all the circumstances of the case
items.why: The nearest thing in statute to protection for a careful director, and it is discretionary: where an officer is or may be liable for negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust but acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused, the court may relieve him wholly or in part. Records are how reasonableness is shown; the section does not say so.

items.title: Practice Direction 57AD: Disclosure in the Business and Property Courts
items.locator: Paras 2.2, 2.5-2.6 (meaning of document), 3.1 (disclosure duties), 4.1-4.5 (preservation), 13.1 (native format, metadata)
items.quote: It also extends to metadata, and other embedded data which is not typically visible on screen or a printout.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. In the Business and Property Courts of England and Wales, a person who knows it is or may become a party to proceedings must take reasonable steps to preserve relevant documents, including those a retention policy would otherwise delete, and must disclose known adverse documents. Documents include deleted information and metadata, so a record's creation date is itself evidence. Page shows 'Updated: Thursday, 29 September 2022'. Practice Direction 31B, read alongside, applies similar preservation duties elsewhere.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.locator: Section 2 ('ATRS purpose and scope'); sections 5-13 (the template tiers)
items.quote: Enable senior responsible owners to take meaningful accountability for algorithmic tools and their outputs
items.why: A ready-made structure for a per-system record: owner and responsibility, description and rationale, deployment context, tool and model specification, data, risks, mitigations and impact assessments. Mandatory by policy, not statute, for government departments and for arm's length bodies delivering public services, for tools with a significant influence on decisions with public effect. Updated 8 May 2025.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 5.1 (GOVERN), document page 22 (page 27 of the PDF); MAP 2.2; MEASURE 3.1
items.quote: Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes, and bolster accountability in AI system teams.
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that treats documentation as part of governance, not an afterthought: roles, system limits, test results and risk tracking are each to be documented. Also says processes for independent review can reduce internal bias.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 8 ('Document your data, models and prompts'), provisions 8.1 and 8.1.1
items.quote: Developers shall document and maintain a clear audit trail of their system design and post-deployment maintenance plans.
items.why: A voluntary government code. Developers keep an audit trail of design and maintenance plans and pass documentation down to operators, covering sources of training data, intended scope and limitations, guardrails, retention time and failure modes. Tells a buyer what record to ask a supplier for.

items.title: AI Act, Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.locator: Article 26(5)-(6); 'About this text' notice. Article 73 (serious incident reporting) read alongside
items.quote: Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control
items.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page); it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026. Deployers of high-risk systems must keep automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months. On the Commission's copy of Article 113 these high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. Relevant only to organisations within the Act's reach.

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 3: Documentation
items.locator: 'At a glance' and 'Checklist'; sections 'What documentation should we provide to demonstrate the explainability of our AI system?' and 'How should we organise this documentation?'; under-review banner
items.quote: It is essential to document each stage of the process behind the design and deployment of an AI decision-support system
items.why: The regulator's guidance on what an AI decision file should hold, stage by stage from design to the decision given to the individual, including an audit trail of who received explanations. The closest UK regulator text to the criterion's 'filed per system' standard. Guidance, not law, and it reaches AI only where personal data is used. The page carries a banner that it is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act, and it still refers to 'the GDPR' and Article 22, which UK law has since replaced with Articles 22A-22D. No date is printed on the page; the year given is that of the guidance's first publication and was not confirmed on the page today.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 9.1: General rules on record-keeping
items.locator: SYSC 9.1.1R (dated 01/01/2021); SYSC 9.1.1AR and 9.1.1BR (common platform firms: compliance, risk management and internal audit reports to be kept)
items.quote: must arrange for orderly records to be kept of its business and internal organisation
items.why: A binding regulator rule that sets the 'regulator-grade' test in terms: records must be sufficient to enable the FCA to monitor the firm's compliance. For common platform firms each compliance, risk management and internal audit report to senior management must be kept. Sector-specific (FCA-authorised firms); not written for AI, but an AI system used in a regulated activity falls within 'business and internal organisation'.

items.title: AI Act, Article 18: Documentation keeping (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.locator: Article 18(1)(a)-(e); read with Article 12 (automatic logging over the lifetime of the system)
items.quote: for a period ending 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service
items.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal; it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version of the AI Act as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes. The provider of a high-risk system must keep its technical documentation, quality management documentation and declaration of conformity available to authorities for ten years. A provider duty, so it tells a UK deployer what record a supplier within the Act's reach must hold and can be asked for; the deployer's own log duty is Article 26, already on this list. High-risk rules are not yet in application.

items.title: Code of Practice on the management of records issued under section 46 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000
items.locator: Paragraph 1.2.4; paragraph 1.3 (status of the Code); Glossary ('Records', citing BS ISO 15489-1:2016)
items.quote: Authorities should manage their information so as to create and maintain a record of their activities which, in turn, provides evidence of their activities.
items.why: The statutory code on keeping, managing and destroying records, and a free statement of the records-management principles that the paid standard BS ISO 15489 sets out. Defines a record as information kept as evidence. A statutory code for public authorities under the Freedom of Information Act (the publication page says it applies to England, Northern Ireland and Wales); a benchmark for others. It does not mention algorithms or AI. Published 15 July 2021.

items.title: SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 3.5 ('Model development documentation'), points (a) and (b); para 1.5 (in effect 17 May 2024)
items.quote: Firms should have comprehensive, and up-to-date documentation on the design, theory, and logic underlying the development of their models.
items.why: A supervisor's test of whether a model file is good enough: detailed enough that an independent third party with the relevant expertise could understand how the model operates, covering data sources and quality tests, choice of method and assumptions, and with enough detail on vendor models to validate the firm's use of them. Applies to banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval; a benchmark elsewhere, not a rule.

items.title: Government Response: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
items.publisher: Australian Government, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet
items.locator: Recommendation 23.8 ('Documenting decisions and discussions') and the Government's response
items.quote: should develop standards for documenting important decisions and discussions, and the delivery of training on those standards
items.why: An official inquiry into an automated decision scheme concluding that decisions were not properly recorded. The Royal Commission recommended standards for documenting important decisions and discussions, with training; the Australian Government accepted this and tied record-keeping to integrity. Read in the Government's response, which reproduces the recommendation: the Royal Commission's own site did not respond today, so its findings of fact on missing records were not read. Australian public service, not UK companies.

items.title: Reviewable Automated Decision-Making: A Framework for Accountable Algorithmic Systems
items.publisher: Jennifer Cobbe, Michelle Seng Ah Lee and Jatinder Singh (arXiv; ACM FAccT 2021)
items.quote: determining the contextually appropriate record-keeping mechanisms to facilitate meaningful review - both of individual decisions and of the process as a whole
items.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read on the authors' arXiv copy. Argues that explanations of a model are not enough for oversight; what a reviewer needs is records of the whole decision process, human and technical, from commissioning to consequences, on the pattern of administrative law. The research basis for a per-system file that covers approvals and reviews as well as the model. A framework, not an empirical test.

items.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
items.publisher: Margaret Mitchell and eight co-authors (arXiv; FAT* 2019)
items.quote: we recommend that released models be accompanied by documentation detailing their performance characteristics
items.why: The paper that established the short standard document for a model: intended use, how it was evaluated, and measured performance across groups. The origin of the supplier documentation a buyer should ask for and file. Peer-reviewed conference paper read on arXiv; it proposes a format and shows two examples and does not test whether model cards improve outcomes.

items.title: Datasheets for Datasets
items.publisher: Timnit Gebru and six co-authors (arXiv; Communications of the ACM, December 2021)
items.quote: The machine learning community currently has no standardized process for documenting datasets, which can lead to severe consequences in high-stakes domains.
items.why: The companion standard for training data: every dataset documented for its motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses. Supplies the 'on what evidence' part of an approval file where a system was trained or tuned on the organisation's or a supplier's data. Published article read on the authors' arXiv copy; a proposal, with no test of effect, and the statement about the absence of a standard process dates from 2018-2021.
